title: Maharashtra's Varkari
hook: a man with a gray beard, soaked from the rain, calls the god he's walking to 'mother'

segments.voice: Yesterday, Maharashtra's Varkari and Pundalik's brick: a god who waits, hands on hips, while a son finishes his care. What did you finish all the way through? Day one thousand three hundred eighty-four.

A man with a gray beard, soaked from the rain, stops at the side of the road to tie his sandal. When he stands up again, he lifts his arms and calls out, not to a friend, but to the god at the end of the road. And the word he uses is mother. Vithu mauli. Vitthal, mother. Nobody around him finds that strange. The god he's walking toward is shown as a man standing on a brick, and here is an old man calling him mother. Today, the names Varkaris give their god, and why one of them is mother.
screen: `A GRAY BEARD IN THE RAIN.` → `HE CALLS OUT: MOTHER.` → `VITHU MAULI.`

segments.voice: The god of Pandharpur has more than one name, and each one is a different way of coming close. Vitthal is the name on the temple. Vithoba adds a touch of affection, the way a family turns a name into a nickname. Pandurang is another, and Varkaris hear in all of them the same god, a form of Krishna, standing on his brick. Then there's mauli. In Marathi it's a tender word for mother, and Varkari songs use it for Vitthal. Why mother, for a god shown as a man? Because of what a mother is to a child. You don't need to be worthy to run to her. You don't need the right words or the right clothes. You come tired, wet and hungry, and she takes you in. That's the relationship the Varkari saints sang about. In songs tradition gives to Namdev and Tukaram, the singer calls out to Vitthal this way: as a child calls a mother, without ceremony. And the word doesn't stop with God. Varkaris call Jnaneshwar mauli too, and the cry Jnanoba Mauli rises from the road. And here's one more turn: on the road, pilgrims call one another mauli. A stranger offering you tea is mauli. The person whose feet you bow to is mauli. So the same tender word runs from the god, to the saint, to the person walking next to you. It's a whole way of seeing, packed into one word. If the god at the end of the road is a mother, then the people on the road with you are family.
screen: `VITTHAL, VITHOBA, PANDURANG` · `MAULI: MOTHER` · `THE SAINT IS MAULI TOO` · `THE STRANGER BESIDE YOU, MAULI`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath slow. Bring to mind someone who took you in when you came to them tired: a parent, a grandparent, a friend, a teacher. Notice what it felt like to arrive without needing the right words. Stay with that. Then, as the minute goes on, let that same warmth widen, to one stranger you saw today. If you pray, you can call God by whatever tender name your own tradition gives. The bell holds the time.
Maharashtra's Varkari. The tradition that calls its god Vithu mauli, mother, and calls the pilgrim next to it mauli too. Today's word.
Your line: Maharashtra's Varkari. Today, greet one stranger as warmly as you'd greet family, even if it's only with your eyes. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-four.

howItsDone: Varkaris call Vitthal by tender names such as Vithoba and Vithu mauli, cry out 'Jnanoba Mauli' on the road, and address fellow pilgrims as mauli.

fork.setup: you're on the road to Pandharpur. a stranger hands you a cup of tea and calls you mauli. what do you say back?
options: correct them: you're not their mother.
thank them and call them mauli too.

original.note: Vitthal in Marathi, written in Devanagari: the god of Pandharpur, also called Vithoba and Pandurang.

trapdoor: what you thought: mauli is a name for a mother at home.
what it means: Varkaris use it for Vitthal, for the saint Jnaneshwar, and for one another on the road.
what a scholar hears: one word of tenderness turning a god, a saint and a crowd of strangers into a single family.

sources.ref: Varkari names for Vitthal (Vithoba, Pandurang, Vithu mauli); 'Jnanoba Mauli' and mauli as a form of address on the wari
abhangs of Namdev and Tukaram addressing Vitthal as mother

notes: 'mauli' glossed as a tender Marathi word for mother (from mau-li, often linked to Sanskrit mātṛ): confirm the gloss; no root claim made in the script.
'Pilgrims often call one another mauli' on the wari: widely reported, but confirm.
Namdev and Tukaram addressing Vitthal as mother: confirm that abhangs by each use mauli/aai for Vitthal.
'a form of Krishna': Varkaris identify Vitthal with Krishna (and Vishnu); confirm phrasing.
Original: विठ्ठल; pronunciation guide 'VIT-thul' is approximate (retroflex double tth).
